fbd-statics.claim: Statics is balance: a body in equilibrium has ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 about ANY point. The free-body diagram is the method — draw the body alone with all external forces, choose a pivot that kills unknowns (torque = r⊥·F), then write the two sum equations.
fbd-statics.probe: A 0.4 m beam is pinned at its left end, rests on a roller 0.3 m from the pin, and carries a 50 N load at the right end. Draw the FBD, choose a pivot, and find the roller reaction and the pin's reactions.
rubric: FBD drawn with all external forces: pin reactions, roller normal, 50 N load
Στ about the pin: R·0.3 = 50·0.4 → R = 66.7 N
ΣF balance gives pin forces: V = 50 − 66.7 = −16.7 N, H = 0
torque = r⊥·F used consistently with correct sign
fbd-statics.transfer_probe: A bookshelf leans against a wall, held by a single bracket screw. Draw the shelf alone with all external forces, pick the pivot that kills the most unknowns, and write the two balance equations — where does the wall push?

practice.problem_frame: Given a beam/bracket with known geometry, loads, and supports, produce a correct FBD and solve for unknown reactions.
practice.discriminates_from: Moment balance about a point that does not kill unknowns, or summing forces without a diagram.
practice.verify: Take a finished FBD, recompute Στ about a different pivot — the answers must match; check units N and N·m.
error_bank: torque computed with the full distance instead of the perpendicular component
sign errors from inconsistent pivot convention
forgetting that the roller only provides a normal force

stress-strain.claim: The tensile curve is the material's report card: stress = force/area, strain = elongation/length. Below yield it returns (elastic); past yield it stays deformed (plastic); ultimate is the peak; fracture ends it. Design keeps working stress below yield with a factor of safety — and fatigue kills well below yield under cycling.
stress-strain.probe: A 6061-T6 part (yield 276 MPa, endurance limit ≈ 95 MPa) sees (a) 40 MPa static and (b) 40 ± 20 MPa cyclic. Give the verdict for each with the factor of safety or fatigue check, and explain why 'it's below yield so it's safe' is wrong for case (b).
rubric: static: FoS = 276/40 ≈ 6.9 — safe
cyclic: peak 60 MPa but amplitude matters — amplitude 20 MPa vs endurance 95 MPa → safe, yet yield alone cannot decide
explains fatigue is a cycling/amplitude phenomenon that occurs below yield
names stress = F/A and strain = ΔL/L

viz.hint: Draggable working-stress marker on an interactive stress-strain curve with yield/ultimate/fracture zones; toggle from static to cyclic and watch the allowed zone collapse to the endurance limit.

stress-strain.transfer_probe: A team absorbs one crunch week elastically but deforms under sustained overload, and repeated crunch cycles burn people out far below the single-sprint limit. Map yield, plastic deformation, factor of safety, and fatigue onto team load planning — where is the endurance limit in this picture?

microstructure-failure.claim: Material behavior comes from the grain scale. Metals are crystal lattices — FCC, BCC, HCP — whose dislocations slide under stress; that sliding IS plastic deformation, and it is why metals bend instead of shatter. Work hardening (cold working) jams dislocations, raising yield at the cost of ductility. The ductile-brittle transition makes BCC steels brittle when cold while FCC (austenitic steel, aluminum) stays tough. Hardness, toughness, and strength measure different things: a hard file is brittle; a tough spring absorbs impact.
microstructure-failure.probe: A steel gear shatters on a cold test bench but bends warm. Name the phenomenon and the lattice behavior behind it. Then explain why cold-worked aluminum is stronger but less forgiving, and distinguish hardness, toughness, and strength in one sentence each.
rubric: ductile-brittle transition: BCC steels turn brittle as temperature drops; FCC (austenitic, aluminum) stays ductile
dislocations: plastic flow = dislocation motion; work hardening jams them → higher yield, lower ductility
hardness = resistance to indentation; toughness = energy absorbed before fracture; strength = stress at yield/break — a hard material can be brittle

viz.hint: A Charpy-style notch test: the same steel at 20°C (bent) and −40°C (shattered), with a dislocation line gliding through the FCC lattice and stuck in the BCC one.

materials-selection.claim: Material choice is a requirements filter, not a favorite: list constraints (strength, stiffness, weight, cost, corrosion), then eliminate. 6061-T6 is not 'aluminum' — the temper is part of the spec. Polymers creep under sustained load; dissimilar metals corrode galvanically in humidity; fasteners carry load by preload, not by their own shear strength.
materials-selection.probe: A bracket spans 100 mm, carries 50 N in bending, must be light, cheap, and live near a warm garage. Compare 6061-T6, PETG, and mild steel: state the filter you applied, your pick, and the one risk you flag for the part.
rubric: runs a requirements filter (strength + stiffness for the span/load, weight, cost) rather than intuition
makes a defensible pick with numeric reasoning (e.g., PETG creep or 6061 FoS)
flags a real risk: creep, corrosion, or temper

practice.problem_frame: Given a part's loads, geometry, environment, and a materials table, run an elimination and defend one choice with numbers.
practice.discriminates_from: Picking by experience ('aluminum is good') without translating loads into stress/stiffness checks.
practice.verify: Recompute stress from the chosen material's section properties; check the risk you flagged against its datasheet.
error_bank: ignoring creep for a sustained polymer load
mating dissimilar metals without a corrosion thought

manufacturing-dfma.claim: Every process imprints constraints: 3D printing — overhangs, anisotropy, layer lines; CNC — tool reach, radiused internal corners, fixturing; sheet metal — bend radius and springback; casting — draft and shrinkage. DFMA: fewer parts, symmetric parts, easy access, standard hardware — every part must justify its existence. Tolerance economy: ±0.5 mm is nearly free, ±0.005 mm is expensive — tighten only where function demands. Joining: welding, adhesive, rivets each have a job; surface treatments (anodize, powder coat) are part of the design.
manufacturing-dfma.probe: You are printing a bracket on a 3D printer: name the three failure modes you design against. Then take a 4-part, 6-screw assembly and apply DFMA: what rule do you apply and what is one concrete consolidation? A part drawn at ±0.5 mm everywhere is cheap and one at ±0.005 mm is not — say why, and name two joining methods besides screws with a use for each. Finally: which surface treatment for an aluminum part, for corrosion-resistant aesthetics, for stainless — and what does each buy?
rubric: three print constraints: overhang support, layer adhesion/anisotropy, elephant foot or warping
DFMA rule stated: minimize part count / symmetry / standard hardware
a concrete consolidation (e.g., merge two parts or add a locating feature so screws self-align)
tolerance economy: loose tolerances are nearly free, tight ones drive process cost nonlinearly — tighten only where function needs it
joining: welding (permanent, strong, distortion risk), adhesive (distributes load, dissimilar materials), rivets/pins (semi-permanent, shear)
surface treatments: anodize (aluminum — wear/corrosion), powder coat (corrosion/aesthetics), passivation (stainless)

machine-elements.claim: Machine elements are the load paths you don't see: bearings carry radial/axial load with fits that must not creep on the shaft, and their life is finite — L10 life is when 10% of a population has failed, and it falls with load cubed. Fasteners work by preload (torque → preload → clamp force), not by the bolt's own shear. A gearbox trades speed for torque while reflected inertia scales with the ratio squared. Tolerance stack-ups decide whether parts meet at all — and a round-looking bore isn't round: geometric callouts (roundness, position) govern the real fit, not the nominal size.
machine-elements.probe: You pick a 10:1 planetary for the QDD: how does the motor's rotor inertia appear at the output, and why does that matter for backdrivability? Then: you torque a joint screw to spec — what are you actually setting, and why does preload matter more than the screw's ultimate strength? The output bearing sees a radial load — what does L10 life mean and what does it depend on? Finally: two parts that must meet — worst-case or statistical stack-up, and which drawing callouts decide whether they actually assemble?
rubric: reflected inertia × n² (10:1 → rotor inertia ×100 at output)
explains why high reflected inertia fights backdrivability (hand-pushing the output)
torque sets preload; preload sets clamp force; joint strength = preload, not bolt shear
bearing L10: life at which 10% of a population has failed; falls with load³
stack-up awareness: worst-case vs statistical assembly; geometric callouts (roundness/position) decide whether parts actually meet

gruebler-dof.claim: Degrees of freedom count independent motions: DOF = 3(n−1) − 2j₁ − j₂ for planar mechanisms, where n = links including ground, j₁ = 1-DOF joints (pins, sliders), j₂ = 2-DOF joints (cam pairs). Draw the kinematic diagram first — links as lines, joints as symbols — then count.
gruebler-dof.probe: Draw kinematic diagrams for (a) a four-bar with 4 links and 4 pin joints, and (b) a slider-crank with 3 pins and 1 slider. Compute DOF for both and interpret what the number means for how many inputs you need.
rubric: slider-crank: 3(4−1) − 2·4 = 1 (n = 4, j₁ = 4)
kinematic diagrams drawn with links as lines and joints as symbols
interprets DOF = 1 as 'one input drives the mechanism'
gruebler-dof.transfer_probe: An office chair: seat, backrest, gas lift, five-star base with caster wheels. Draw links as lines and joints as symbols, then count DOF — which joints are pins/sliders (j1) and which are rolling contacts (j2)?

practice.problem_frame: Given a mechanism sketch, draw its kinematic diagram and compute DOF with Gruebler's criterion.
practice.discriminates_from: Counting parts instead of links, or forgetting that ground is a link.
practice.verify: Re-count n and j₁ against the diagram; the formula output should match the obvious mobility (e.g., a four-bar is driven by one input).
error_bank: forgetting ground counts as a link
counting a cam joint as j₁ instead of j₂
miscounting sliders as eliminating a link

grashof-fourbar.claim: A four-bar's behavior is decided by one inequality: if shortest + longest ≤ sum of the other two, at least one link can make a full revolution (Grashof); if not, no link fully rotates (non-Grashof — everything rocks). Grounding different links changes the outcome: crank-rocker, double-crank, or double-rocker.
grashof-fourbar.probe: Links are 20, 30, 35, 45 mm in consecutive order. Check the Grashof condition. Then say what motion you get with the 20 mm link grounded, and with the 45 mm link grounded (shortest acting as a side link). State the adjacency assumption you used. Name all four outcomes.
rubric: s + l = 20 + 45 = 65 ≤ p + q = 30 + 35 = 65 — Grashof (equality counts)
shortest (20) grounded → double-crank (both side links fully rotate)
longest (45) grounded with shortest as an adjacent side link → crank-rocker (the shortest side link cranks); states the adjacency assumption since outcome depends on assembly, not lengths alone
names all four: crank-rocker, double-crank, double-rocker, non-Grashof rocker

viz.hint: Adjustable-linkage sandbox: drag the four bar lengths and watch the condition flip — full cranks turn red, rockers oscillate. The inequality is the toggle.

grashof-fourbar.transfer_probe: A desk lamp has two arms joined like a four-bar, with its base screwed to the desk. Given its bar lengths, which joints can fully rotate — and what changes if you unbolt it and fix a different bar to the desk instead? State the inequality you checked.

mechanism-drives.claim: The rigid-body drive bank. Slider-crank: rotation → reciprocation, with dead-center positions the mechanism must be driven through. Scotch yoke: rotation → pure sinusoidal reciprocation, simpler but hard on the pin. Lead vs ball screw: rotation → linear; the ball screw is backdrivable, the lead screw self-locks (holds position with power off). Belt vs chain: parallel shafts at a ratio — a belt slips to protect the drivetrain, a chain is positive (no slip) but needs tension and lubrication.
mechanism-drives.probe: For each of: slider-crank, scotch yoke, lead screw vs ball screw, belt vs chain — name the input motion, the output motion, and one real-world use or the property that decides between the pair.
rubric: slider-crank: rotation → reciprocation (engine piston)
scotch yoke: rotation → sinusoidal reciprocation (pump)
ball screw backdrivable vs lead screw self-locking (CNC vs vertical axes that must hold position)
belt: slip-to-protect, needs tension; chain: positive drive, no slip, needs tension and lube

mechanism-special.claim: The special-motion bank. Cam-follower: rotation → a programmed motion profile — the pressure angle must stay below ~30° or the follower jams. Geneva: continuous rotation → intermittent steps, with a jerk spike at lock. Ratchet: reciprocation → one-way steps. Oldham coupling: transmits rotation across a small parallel offset. Universal joint: transmits rotation through an angle, but the output speed oscillates twice per revolution — a double Cardan fixes it. Planetary gear: one stage, three ports (sun, ring, carrier) with the ratio set by which is held.
mechanism-special.probe: Name the input and output motion of: cam, Geneva, ratchet, Oldham, universal joint, planetary. For the U-joint give the one thing that makes a single joint unsuitable at constant speed, and for the cam give the angle that must stay bounded.
rubric: cam: rotation → programmed profile; pressure angle below ~30° (jamming/undercutting beyond)
Geneva: continuous → intermittent indexing; jerk spike at lock
ratchet: reciprocating → one-way step
Oldham: parallel-offset coupling, no angular change
U-joint: output speed oscillates 2× per revolution; double Cardan/homokinetic joint fixes it
planetary: sun/ring/carrier ports; ratio depends on which member is held

metrology-uncertainty.claim: A measurement without uncertainty is a guess: resolution ≠ accuracy ≠ precision. Uncertainty is budgeted — Type A from repeated readings (standard deviation of the mean), Type B from instrument specs (calibration), combined root-sum-square, reported with k=2 (95%). The caliper's 0.01 mm resolution says nothing about its 0.05 mm accuracy.
metrology-uncertainty.probe: You measure a shaft five times with a caliper: 10.02, 10.00, 10.01, 10.03, 10.00 mm. Compute the mean, Type A (s/√n), assume Type B = 0.05 mm, combine RSS, and report with k=2. Then explain the resolution/accuracy distinction.
rubric: mean = 10.012 mm
Type A = s/√5 ≈ 0.006 mm
resolution is the readout step, accuracy is the calibration truth — a 0.01 mm display can still lie by 0.05 mm

practice.problem_frame: Given a set of repeated readings and an instrument accuracy, produce a k=2 uncertainty statement.
practice.discriminates_from: Reporting the resolution or the spread as 'the measurement'. Both understate the true uncertainty.
practice.verify: The combined uncertainty must be ≥ each individual contributor; sanity-check the ± with the largest source dominating.
error_bank: using s instead of s/√n for the mean
adding uncertainties arithmetically instead of RSS

fem-intuition.claim: FEA is a machine for approximating, not for truth: the part is cut into small elements, each with a simple assumed displacement field, glued together by continuity, and solved as one big linear system. Answer quality depends on mesh density, element type, and honest boundary conditions — the solver will happily compute a wrong answer.
fem-intuition.probe: Your CAD tool's stress simulation says a bracket fails at 200 N, but your hand calc says 500 N. Give three likely reasons the FEA is wrong, in order of likelihood, and what you would do to check each.
rubric: mesh density/convergence check (refine until the answer stops changing)
boundary condition honesty — where and how the part is actually fixed/loaded
load idealization — point loads create infinite stress at the node
hand-calc cross-check as the arbiter

viz.hint: A bracket mesh slider: coarse vs fine vs converged stress contour; plus a knob that 'moves the bolt hole' to show stress singularity. Caption: 'the solver trusts your BCs.'

fem-intuition.transfer_probe: An election model aggregates precinct samples and happily outputs a confident but wrong forecast. Name the mesh-density, boundary-condition, and hand-calc-cross-check analogues in polling — what would you refine or verify before trusting it?

dfma-joining-surface.claim: Joints are picked by load and reversibility — welding for permanent high-strength joints, adhesive for distributed load across dissimilar materials, rivets for shear-loaded semi-permanent joints — and finishes by substrate: anodize for aluminum wear and corrosion, powder coat for corrosion plus color and aesthetics, passivation for stainless corrosion without a coating.
dfma-joining-surface.probe: Three seams need joining: a permanent high-strength steel seam, a dissimilar-materials seam carrying distributed load, and a shear-loaded seam that may be disassembled. Assign welding, adhesive, or rivets to each and say why. Then pick the finish for a bare aluminum part, a steel part needing a colorful corrosion-resistant skin, and a stainless part, stating what each finish buys.
rubric: assigns the joints correctly: permanent high-strength to welding, dissimilar distributed-load to adhesive, shear-loaded removable to rivets or pins
justifies each joint by load path and reversibility, including a real drawback (welding distortion, adhesive surface prep, rivet holes)
maps each finish to its substrate and payoff: anodize on aluminum for wear and corrosion, powder coat for corrosion plus color and aesthetics, passivation on stainless for corrosion without a film
dfma-joining-surface.transfer_probe: A theater costume needs three seams — a permanent load-bearing harness seam, a delicate mixed-fabric applique, a replaceable armor plate — plus three fabric treatments for nylon, cotton, and treated wool. Pick stitching, fabric glue, or snaps for each seam with why, and map each treatment to its fabric and payoff.

dfma-partcount-tolerance.claim: Cheap, buildable designs use fewer symmetric parts with standard hardware so assembly is unambiguous, and spend tight tolerances only where function demands because precision cost rises steeply.
dfma-partcount-tolerance.probe: A 4-part bracket held by 6 screws must be redesigned for cheaper build and assembly. State the DFMA rules you apply and describe one concrete consolidation of this assembly. Its drawing has faces at ±0.5 mm and one bore at ±0.005 mm: say what each tolerance costs to hold and which you keep tight versus loosen.
rubric: states DFMA rules: minimize part count, prefer symmetric or self-locating parts, use standard hardware
describes one concrete consolidation (e.g. merge two parts, add a locating feature so screws self-align) and what it eliminates
tolerance economy: ±0.5 mm is nearly free while ±0.005 mm is expensive, so loosen the faces and keep tight only the bore whose function needs it
dfma-partcount-tolerance.transfer_probe: A soup recipe has 12 steps, 6 specialty ingredients, and calls for seasoning to the gram but timing to the nearest half hour. Apply part-count reduction and tolerance economy: which steps or ingredients do you consolidate or standardize, and where do you measure precisely versus loosely?

dfma-process-limits.claim: Every process imprints a geometric limit: FDM printing needs supported overhangs and is weak between layers with warping risk, CNC milling is bounded by tool reach with radiused internal corners and fixturing, sheet metal needs a minimum bend radius with springback, and casting needs draft angles plus shrinkage allowance.
dfma-process-limits.probe: The same bracket will be made four ways: FDM print, CNC mill, bent sheet, and sand casting. For each of the four processes, name the key geometric limit that shapes the design and the defect or failure you get if you ignore it.
rubric: FDM: overhang/support-angle limit plus interlayer weakness (anisotropy) and warping or elephant foot
CNC: cutting depth bounded by tool reach and diameter, internal corners keep the tool radius, part needs fixturing
sheet: minimum bend radius for the thickness plus springback compensation
casting: draft angles for release plus shrinkage allowance
dfma-process-limits.transfer_probe: A kitchen makes the same dish by deep-frying, steaming, and baking. For each method state its shaping limit and the failure you get ignoring it — then map overhang/support, tool reach, bend radius, and draft onto this kitchen.

mel-bearings-l10.claim: A rolling bearing's L10 life is the life at which 10% of an identical population has failed by rolling-contact fatigue (90% survive), scaling as (C/P)^3 in million revolutions — so double the load and life falls eightfold — and a bearing is correctly sized only when its L10 hours at operating speed exceed the service target.
mel-bearings-l10.probe: A catalog rates a deep-groove bearing at dynamic load rating C = 10 kN. Your shaft applies P = 2 kN at 1000 rpm and the gearbox must survive 5000 h. What does the L10 rating actually promise, how does life change if you double the load, and does this bearing meet the target? Show the calculation.
rubric: states L10 is the life at which 10% of a population has failed by fatigue (90% survive), not a guarantee for one bearing
computes L10 = (C/P)^3 = 125 million revolutions ≈ 2083 h at 1000 rpm, giving the verdict: fails the 5000 h target
states doubling the load cuts life eightfold (cubic dependence), not by half
mel-bearings-l10.transfer_probe: A laundromat chain buys 200 identical washers whose drum bearings are catalog-rated L10 = 8000 h at the rated spin load. Half the stores chronically overload the drums so the bearing load doubles. What fraction of machines do you expect to need a bearing swap before 8000 h at normal load, how long will the overloaded bearings last, and which rated number decides whether the fleet survives the 5-year lease?

mel-gear-inertia.claim: A reduction of ratio n reflects motor-side inertia to the output as n² times its own value, so a high-ratio joint carries a large apparent inertia at the link and resists being backdriven by hand.
mel-gear-inertia.probe: A robot joint uses a motor with rotor inertia 5e-5 kg·m² behind a 10:1 planetary. What inertia does a hand pushing the output feel from the rotor alone, and what does that imply for backdrivability versus the same motor coupled direct-drive? Show the scaling.
rubric: computes reflected inertia = n²·Jm = 100 × 5e-5 = 5e-3 kg·m² felt at the output
states the scaling is the square of the ratio, not the ratio itself
concludes the 10:1 joint resists backdriving because the hand must accelerate 100× the rotor inertia, while direct-drive feels only the bare rotor inertia and stays backdrivable
mel-gear-inertia.transfer_probe: A cordless screwdriver has a 50:1 planetary behind a light motor; its direct-drive sibling couples an equivalent motor straight to the bit. Which one can you twist backwards by hand with the power off, how does the motor's inertia appear at the bit in each, and what scaling decides the difference?

mel-preload.claim: Tightening torque stretches the bolt into a stiff spring via T = K·F·d, clamping the plates with force F; external shear is then carried by friction between the clamped plates, so a preloaded joint holds by clamp force while the bolt itself stays out of shear.
mel-preload.probe: You torque an M6 steel bolt (d = 6 mm, nut factor K = 0.2) to T = 6 N·m to clamp two plates that must resist a 500 N shear load. What clamp force did you set, what physically holds the joint when the shear arrives, and why would the same bolt finger-tight fail the joint despite identical ultimate strength? Show the calculation.
rubric: computes preload F = T/(K·d) = 6/(0.2 × 0.006) = 5000 N of clamp force
states friction between the clamped plates carries the 500 N shear while the bolt shank stays in tension, not shear
explains finger-tight means near-zero preload so the plates slip and the bolt falls into shear/bending and loosening — ultimate strength alone cannot save a joint with no clamp
mel-preload.transfer_probe: Your bicycle's stem clamps the handlebar with two M5 bolts torqued to spec, and the bar must survive pothole tugs that try to twist it. What did the torque wrench actually set, what holds the bar when a tug arrives, and why would the same bolts finger-tight let the bar slip even though their ultimate strength is unchanged?

mel-stackup-gdt.claim: Whether stacked parts assemble is decided by the tolerance stack, not the nominal: a worst-case stack adds tolerances linearly and guarantees assembly only when the worst combination still clears, while a statistical (RSS) stack combines them as root-sum-square and predicts high-yield assembly at looser, cheaper tolerances — and where size tolerances leave form and location free, roundness and position callouts bound the bore lobing and hole-center shift that actually jam the fit.
mel-stackup-gdt.probe: Three plates stack, each thickness ±0.10 mm, with a nominal 0.25 mm gap left for a cover; the stack is pinned through holes that carry a position callout, and the pin runs in bores that carry a roundness callout. Compute the worst-case gap stack and the RSS gap stack, give the assemble-or-jam verdict under each, and state what shape error each callout (roundness, position) bounds.
rubric: worst-case stack ±0.30 mm → minimum gap 0.25 − 0.30 = −0.05 mm → predicts a possible jam, so assembly is not guaranteed
RSS stack √(3 × 0.10²) ≈ 0.17 mm → minimum gap ≈ +0.08 mm → predicts assembly at high but not 100% yield
position bounds hole-center offset from true position (decides whether pins pass stacked holes); roundness bounds bore lobing and ovality (decides shaft fit even when the diameter measures correctly)
mel-stackup-gdt.transfer_probe: A flat-pack wardrobe pins three stacked particle boards with dowels through clearance holes; each board thickness varies ±0.5 mm and the drilled holes wander and come out slightly oval. State the calculation that promises every unit assembles versus the one that promises most units assemble, and state which drawing note you tighten when dowels miss their holes versus when a dowel binds in a hole that measures the right diameter.

capstone.claim: You can USE Mechatronics — Mechanical Engineering in your own work, not just explain it.
capstone.probe: Build the thing. In your real repo, your real notes, your real argument — produce something that only works if you actually understand Mechatronics — Mechanical Engineering. Your stated goal: The cad/ + hardware structural side of the vault roadmap: free-body diagrams and statics, stress-strain through microstructure and failure, materials selection, DFMA, machine elements, mechanism kinematics (Gruebler, Grashof, drive and special mechanisms), FEM intuition, and metrology/uncertainty. Feeds Phase 0 milestones, QDD CAD/FEA in Phase 3, and every load path after. Calculus prerequisite lives in the spine tree.. Ship it, then explain which concept made which decision.
rubric: the artifact exists and works (or the argument stands on its own)
names at least two concepts from this topic that DECIDED something in it
identifies where the model broke down or needed more than the topic gave

precision-fits-gdt.claim: Bearings are located, not just bought: interference on the rotating ring, clearance on the stationary ring (H7/k6-class callouts from the tables, with WHY), anodize growth masked out of bores, axial retention by shoulders/circlips/shims — never hope. Shafts size from combined torsion plus bending, fasteners from grade plus torque. And the drawing speaks GD&T: concentricity of bearing bores, flatness of mating faces, perpendicularity where rotation meets structure, stacked across the bearing-gearbox-shaft chain.
precision-fits-gdt.probe: 20 mm shaft spinning in its bore, housing static: who gets interference, who gets clearance, what callouts, and what must be masked before anodize? Size the shaft for combined load, name the axial-retention hardware plus fastener grade and torque spec, and name the three GD&T callouts the chain needs.
rubric: fit rule with direction (interference-rotating / clearance-stationary) + H7/k6-class callouts + anodize masking + axial retention hardware
shaft from combined torsion+bending with grade+torque fasteners — not diameter-by-feel
concentricity + flatness + perpendicularity called out and stacked across the chain

viz.hint: Apply to the QDD joint or the testbed part; the numbers decide the fit, the finish, and the failure reading.

fea-convergence-gate.claim: FEA is guilty until proven innocent: three mesh densities with the finest two agreeing within 5%, peak stress within 20% of the hand calc, boundary conditions audited (constraint points and point loads lie — singularities read infinite), and only then is the contour plot evidence instead of decoration.
fea-convergence-gate.probe: Your bracket shows 180 MPa at the bolt hole on a coarse mesh. State the three acceptance gates, then say what a jump to 260 MPa at a single node on the finest mesh means and what you do about it.
rubric: 3-density convergence under 5% between finest two — run, not claimed
within 20% of hand calc plus a BC audit naming the idealizations
single-node spike read as singularity until proven otherwise — refine or set aside, never screenshot-and-ship

viz.hint: Apply to the QDD joint or the testbed part; the numbers decide the fit, the finish, and the failure reading.

ashby-fractography-tribology.claim: Selection is indexed, failure is read: Ashby plots (stiffness vs strength per density) pick the arm-link material by tradeoff, not brand; fracture faces testify — dimpled is ductile, granular is brittle, beach marks are fatigue; and wear, notch sensitivity, fracture toughness, coatings, and environment each get their own line on the decision sheet.
ashby-fractography-tribology.probe: Stiff light arm link: pick from aluminum/steel/titanium/CFRP/PLA on the Ashby tradeoff. Read three fractures (dimpled / flat granular / beach marks). Name the separate line each of wear, notch, and environment adds.
rubric: Ashby pick with the stiffness-vs-strength tradeoff stated as indices, not vibes
dimpled=ductile / granular=brittle / beach-marks=fatigue — read, not guessed
wear, notch/fracture-toughness, coatings, environment listed as separate design constraints

viz.hint: Apply to the QDD joint or the testbed part; the numbers decide the fit, the finish, and the failure reading.

leaf-compliant-design.claim: Sometimes the best joint has no joint: a flexure gives designed compliance with zero friction and zero backlash — sized in spring steel or composite against a fatigue life, never assumed in PLA (creep eats the rate). Compliance is a designed stiffness with a life constraint, not a floppy print.
leaf-compliant-design.probe: You need a frictionless pivot of known rate for a sensor mount. Choose the material and kill PLA with the creep argument, state what sets the rate, and state what limits its life plus its inspection-or-replacement plan.
rubric: flexure chosen for zero friction/backlash with rate from geometry plus modulus
PLA killed by creep; spring steel/composite picked with a fatigue-life constraint
life limit stated with an inspection or replacement plan

viz.hint: Apply to the QDD joint or the testbed part; the numbers decide the fit, the finish, and the failure reading.

mechanism-quant-behaviors.claim: Vocabulary names them; numbers govern them: slider-crank dead-centers need the flywheel, cam profiles die past 30-degree pressure angles and at undercutting, Geneva entry acceleration forbids speed, ratchets are not precision (backlash is inherent), yoke motion is pure sine (purer than the crank with its second harmonic), Oldham tolerates offset only, single U-joints pulse twice per rev (phase a second for constant velocity), planetaries split by the held member with load shared across planets, ball screws (~90%, backdrivable, so brake them) beat lead screws (~30-50%, self-locking) on efficiency and lose on holding, and belts punish both loose (skip/slap) and tight (bearing overload).
mechanism-quant-behaviors.probe: Pick three mechanisms and decide each with numbers: carry a crank past dead center, kill a cam profile with pressure angle or undercutting (show which), and decide ball-vs-lead for a gravity-loaded vertical axis with the holding argument. Then state the failure behaviors of Geneva, ratchet, yoke-harmonic, Oldham, and single U-joint, plus the planetary held-member rule with its equation.
